- **self**: Private Cloud Compute trust architecture and verification (15/5)

## Definitions

- [statement] PCC is not end-to-end encrypted against the inference node: the node must read request content to generate a response. In Apple’s Apple-silicon design, the device encrypts directly to attested PCC nodes, while relays and supporting load-balancing services sit outside the decryption boundary. This is a measured processing boundary, not ordinary TLS-only cloud hosting. (high confidence) — https://security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute/ · keywords: Private Cloud Compute trust architecture and verification · also: https://arxiv.org/html/2605.24239

## Structure and components

- [statement] Apple's verifiable-transparency design links device-side attestation to an append-only public log of software measurements and public images for production releases. Apple also offers a Virtual Research Environment that can boot PCC releases and verify log consistency, plus source for selected security-critical components such as CloudAttestation, Thimble, and splunkloggingd. (high confidence) — https://security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute/ · keywords: Private Cloud Compute trust architecture and verification · also: https://security.apple.com/blog/pcc-security-research/, https://security.apple.com/documentation/private-cloud-compute/releasetransparency, https://github.com/apple/security-pcc
- [statement] On 2026-06-08 Apple announced extending PCC beyond Apple data centers to Google Cloud using NVIDIA Confidential Computing, Intel TDX, and Google Titan. Apple says the core PCC requirements remain and that the Google Cloud design treats firmware through application software as part of the trusted computing base, with an append-only hardware ledger and at least two independent vendor roots for components that could exfiltrate data. This is an announced architecture, not evidence that its combined protections have been independently tested against every TEE attack. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-06-08) — https://security.apple.com/blog/expanding-pcc/ · keywords: Private Cloud Compute trust architecture and verification · also: https://consortiumforverifiedcomputing.org/atlas/apple-private-cloud-compute
- [statement] Apple’s public verification artifacts include PCC release measurements and binaries, a public transparency log, a Security Guide, a Virtual Research Environment, and selected security-critical source components. The artifacts let researchers inspect released binaries and exercise PCC software, but they do not provide a complete source tree or reproducible build path for every production binary. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-05-22) — https://security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute/ · keywords: Private Cloud Compute trust architecture and verification · also: https://arxiv.org/html/2605.24239, https://security.apple.com/documentation/private-cloud-compute/verifiabletransparency
- [statement] On June 8, 2026, Apple announced an extension of PCC to Google Cloud using NVIDIA Confidential Computing GPUs, Intel TDX CPUs and Google’s Titan chip. Apple said the same five core requirements would apply, with at least two independent vendor roots of trust for components that could exfiltrate data, and described protections as ramping during a summer preview. That dated announcement does not establish the deployment’s status after the preview. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-06-08) — https://security.apple.com/blog/expanding-pcc/ · keywords: Private Cloud Compute trust architecture and verification · also: https://security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute/

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] For the Apple-silicon PCC flow, Apple documents device-side attestation of the node’s operating system and loaded cryptexes. The client verifies that the measured release has an inclusion proof in a public append-only transparency log before wrapping the request key to that node. The current documentation describes a 14-day release-entry lifetime and a 7-day grace period before a user alert for an unresolved log consistency error. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-23) — https://security.apple.com/documentation/private-cloud-compute/releasetransparency · keywords: Private Cloud Compute trust architecture and verification · also: https://security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute/

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] A report published 2026-10-21 by Grego AI says PCC's ensemble certificate-validation path discarded a requested revocation policy, so a revoked but unexpired node certificate could pass that CRL/OCSP gate if other checks passed. The report says Apple credited the finding and fixed it in 26.4; it describes a reported, fixed issue rather than evidence of current exposure. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-21) — https://grego.ai/reports/apple-x509policy-revocation-admission · keywords: Private Cloud Compute trust architecture and verification
- [statement] Apple’s October 2026 SOC 3 page says an independent examination covered controls for the PCC Provisioning System, including provisioning, ongoing verification and protection of information in compute nodes. It explicitly says the examination did not evaluate AI service performance or integrity, so the audit is scoped assurance about controls rather than a complete evaluation of models or every PCC privacy property. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) — https://support.apple.com/guide/certifications/apple-private-cloud-compute-soc-3-audit-apc95a31b9d8/web · keywords: Private Cloud Compute trust architecture and verification · also: https://arxiv.org/html/2605.24239
- [statement] A peer-reviewed 2026 WiSec study reports that PCC’s published compiled binaries have no reproducible builds or symbols, and that full source is unavailable; the researchers therefore reverse-engineered client components. This limits independent source-to-binary comparison. The study evaluates client behavior and production queries rather than independently auditing the complete server attestation and transparency chain. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-05-22) — https://arxiv.org/html/2605.24239 · keywords: Private Cloud Compute trust architecture and verification · also: https://security.apple.com/documentation/private-cloud-compute/verifiabletransparency

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Apple defines PCC’s stateless requirement as using request data only to fulfill that request, deleting it after the response, and retaining no user data through logging or debugging. Apple describes enforcement measures including per-reboot data-volume key randomization by the Secure Enclave and recycling memory address spaces; these are vendor-described controls, not an independent proof that no implementation defect can retain data. (high confidence) — https://security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute/ · keywords: Private Cloud Compute trust architecture and verification · also: https://arxiv.org/html/2605.24239, https://blog.sentry.security/beyond-prompt-injection-hacking-apples-private-cloud-compute/
- [statement] In Apple's original Apple-silicon design, the attested PCC node is the request decryption trust boundary: load balancers and privacy gateways sit outside it and lack request keys. Apple says the node omits remote shells, interactive debugging, and general-purpose logging, and allows only pre-specified, structured, audited logs and metrics to leave; inference code inside the node still processes request content. (high confidence) — https://security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute/ · keywords: Private Cloud Compute trust architecture and verification · also: https://arxiv.org/html/2605.24239
- [statement] Apple defines non-targetability as preventing a limited compromise from steering a selected user's requests to compromised nodes. Its design uses unlinkable single-use credentials, a third-party OHTTP relay that hides the source IP, and load balancing over a node subset chosen without user identity; independent ACM researchers also describe OHTTP and randomized node selection. (high confidence) — https://security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute/ · keywords: Private Cloud Compute trust architecture and verification · also: https://arxiv.org/html/2605.24239
- [statement] The 2026 ACM WiSec analysis reports that published PCC server binaries lack reproducible builds and symbols. The Consortium for Verified Computing's assessment, reviewed 2026-09-25, says no public independent evaluation has examined the full attestation chain. The public artifacts enable inspection and release matching, but do not establish that every deployed executable is reproducible or that every end-to-end guarantee has been independently proven. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-25) — https://arxiv.org/html/2605.24239 · keywords: Private Cloud Compute trust architecture and verification · also: https://consortiumforverifiedcomputing.org/atlas/apple-private-cloud-compute, https://security.apple.com/blog/pcc-security-research/
- [statement] In a July 31, 2026 report, Sentry researcher Drinor Selmanaj said a path traversal in darwin-init let a malicious archive write root-owned files to a writable PCC research VM volume, redirect telemetry, and expose per-request metadata; the researcher reported that Apple’s VRE verifier treated the tampered and clean configurations identically. Apple’s release notes record CVE-2026-20685 and a path-validation fix in PCC release 5E290.3. The report describes a VRE test, not a compromise of production nodes. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-07-31) — https://blog.sentry.security/beyond-prompt-injection-hacking-apples-private-cloud-compute/ · keywords: Private Cloud Compute trust architecture and verification · also: https://security.apple.com/documentation/private-cloud-compute/releasenotes, https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x835-6gm8-j3h4
- [statement] Apple’s non-targetability design aims to prevent a limited compromise from steering a particular user’s requests to a compromised node. Apple describes anonymous authorization, a third-party OHTTP relay, and selection of a subset of nodes; its current guide also says the relay may expose a rough geographic region and requests may carry basic product and operating-system build headers outside the encrypted payload. Apple cautions that a user distinguishable by these properties could be exposed to a semi-targeted attack. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-23) — https://security.apple.com/documentation/private-cloud-compute/nontargetability · keywords: Private Cloud Compute trust architecture and verification · also: https://security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute/, https://arxiv.org/html/2605.24239, https://security.apple.com/documentation/private-cloud-compute/attacks
